title: Buying 100 shares of every NYSE stock under $1 in 1939
statement: With war spreading in Europe and most advisors predicting further depression, Templeton instructed his broker to buy 100 shares of every stock trading under one dollar on the NYSE — about 104 companies, 34 of them in bankruptcy.
outcome: He quadrupled his money within roughly four years as war-production demand revived the economy; only four of the hundred positions turned out to be losses. The trade became the emblem of maximum-pessimism buying.

title: Pioneering global investment through the Templeton Growth Fund
statement: At a time when Americans were legally free but culturally unwilling to invest abroad, Templeton founded the Templeton Growth Fund in Canada, spending months a year visiting companies in Japan, Europe and later everywhere.
outcome: The fund's 38-year record under Templeton averaged roughly 15% annually; Templeton is credited as the father of global investing and was knighted for his contribution.

title: Japanese equity overweight through the postwar rise
statement: Beginning in the 1960s, when Japan was a frontier market still recovering from war, Templeton toured its companies and invested heavily in a market most Western institutions ignored.
outcome: Japan's rise to the world's second-largest economy multiplied the investments many times over; Templeton reduced the position by the late 1980s as Japanese valuations reached extremes he considered indefensible.

title: Selling Japan at the 1980s bubble peak
statement: By the late 1980s, with the Nikkei approaching 40,000 and Japanese stocks carrying extreme multiples, Templeton systematically exited Japanese equities despite continued institutional enthusiasm for Japan's 'new era.'
outcome: The Nikkei peaked at 38,915 on December 29, 1989 and fell more than 60% over the following decade. The exit became a canonical example of selling euphoria that had outrun any defensible value.

title: Calling the internet bubble 'a once-in-a-generation opportunity to short'
statement: Months before the peak, Templeton publicly argued that internet stocks would suffer the greatest wipeout of value in a generation, and put his own money behind zero-coupon bond and short strategies.
outcome: The Nasdaq fell 78% from March 2000 to October 2002; his short positions were reported to have returned roughly 70% for the year.

title: Selling the fund business to Franklin Resources
statement: Templeton sold his asset-management firm, including the Growth Fund franchise, to Franklin Resources, completing his exit from day-to-day management.
outcome: The combined Franklin Templeton organization became one of the largest global asset managers, with over $1.4 trillion under management; the Templeton Foundation received the proceeds powering his philanthropy.

title: Founding the Templeton Prize to honor spiritual progress
statement: Templeton established the prize — originally the Templeton Prize for Progress in Religion — deliberately exceeding the Nobel award in value, arguing that research into spiritual realities deserved equivalent prestige.
outcome: The prize, first awarded to Mother Teresa, has honored the Dalai Lama, Desmond Tutu and leading scientists; the John Templeton Foundation he endowed became a major funder of research at the boundary of science and religion with over $3 billion given.

title: Maximum-pessimism principle — formalizing the buying discipline
statement: Templeton summarized his lifetime method as buying at the point of maximum pessimism — the moment when a company, industry or country is so hated that no bad news remains to be priced — and selling at maximum optimism.
outcome: The aphorism and the practice behind it became the reference point for global contrarian investing; his interview compilations and the Templeton Foundation archives preserve the method in his own words.
